You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Conditions:
        *   $v_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$
        *   $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$
        *   $v_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (startup)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (settled)
    *   The best design so far is `SSHI_FullBridge` (score 77.06).
    *   `SSHI_FullBridge` failures:
        *   S2 (Heavy Load): $v_{pp} = 74.2\text{mV}$ (limit 50mV), $dv = 0.079\text{V}$ (limit 0.02V).
        *   All other conditions passed.
    *   Analysis of `SSHI_FullBridge`:
        *   Full Bridge Rectifier (4x DSCH).
        *   Inductor-switch combo for SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor).
        *   Zener clamp (DZ33) to limit $v_{max}$.
        *   Storage capacitor $C_1$ on `out`.
        *   SSHI part: $L_1$ from `pzp` to `n1`, $S_1$ from `n1` to `pzn`.

    *   S2 has the highest load current ($R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$).
    *   $v_{pp}$ (ripple) and $dv$ (settled) failures in S2 indicate that the storage capacitor $C_1$ is likely too small to maintain the voltage under heavy load, or the charging current is not sufficient to offset the discharge during the period between harvesting pulses.
    *   Wait, the `SSHI_FullBridge` was tuned (48/48 evaluations). The optimizer tried to find the best $C_1, L_1, t_{on}$, etc. If it still fails on ripple/settled for S2, we might need more capacitance or a more efficient power delivery.
    *   However, if we increase $C_1$ too much, $t_{up}$ might increase (startup time).
    *   Looking at the `SSHI_FullBridge` $t_{up}$ for S2: $0.188\text{s}$ (well within $0.4\text{s}$).
    *   Wait, the optimizer already tried to size $C_1$. Let's check the $C_1$ value: $1.8\mu\text{F}$. The maximum allowed $C$ is $47\mu\text{F}$.
    *   If the optimizer stopped at $1.8\mu\text{F}$, it might be because larger values were hurting other conditions (like $t_{up}$ for S4?). Let's check S4 $t_{up}$: $0.258\text{s}$. Still okay.
    *   Maybe the ripple is caused by the nature of the SSHI pulses? No, the rectifier smoothed it.
    *   The "settled" failure ($dv$) means the mean output is still drifting. This usually happens if the capacitor is charging very slowly or if the time constant is too large.

    *   The current SSHI implementation uses a full bridge + a flipping circuit on one side (`pzp` and `pzn`).
    *   In `SSHI_FullBridge`, the $L_1$-$S_1$ branch is in parallel with the piezo. When $S_1$ closes, $L_1$ helps flip the voltage across $C_p$.
    *   Can we improve the energy extraction?
    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge` is very close. The only failure is S2 ripple and stability.
    *   Could a different topology (like a charge pump or a different SSHI variant) be better?
    *   Wait, look at the "HalfBridge_SSHI" result. It failed miserably on stability and ripple.
    *   Let's think about the ripple in S2 for `SSHI_FullBridge`. $v_{pp} = 74.2\text{mV}$. The requirement is $50\text{mV}$. This is quite close.
    *   Maybe the inductor $L_1$ is too small? No, the optimizer handles that.
    *   The problem is that under heavy load (S2), the voltage drops more between pulses.

    *   The `SSHI_FullBridge` is basically a bridge rectifier with an added SSHI flipping circuit.
    *   The SSHI flipping circuit is only on the `pzp`/`pzn` terminals.
    *   Actually, a better way to implement SSHI is often a "Parallel-SSHI" (P-SSHI) or "Series-SSHI" (S-SSHI).
    *   Let's try to introduce a capacitor for the SSHI flipping, but the prompt allows switches and inductors.
    *   Another thought: The current `SSHI_FullBridge` uses a full bridge. Maybe a different rectifier?
    *   Actually, if S2 is the only failure and it's just ripple/settled, increasing $C_1$ should help. Why did the optimizer not increase $C_1$?
    *   $C_{out} = 1.8\mu\text{F}$. Let's check the $v_{avg}$ for S2: $3.28\text{V}$. It's very high (close to the Zener limit).
    *   Ah! If $v_{avg}$ is $3.28\text{V}$, it's sitting right at the Zener breakdown. The Zener `DZ33` is clamping the output.
    *   If the Zener is clamping, the ripple is reduced on the top side but the bottom side is determined by $R_L$ and $C_{out}$.
    *   But the `vpp` is $74\text{mV}$ and $v_{avg}$ is $3.28\text{V}$. If $v_{max}$ is $3.31\text{V}$, then the bottom is $3.31 - 0.074 = 3.236\text{V}$.
    *   The $dv$ failure (settled) means the mean is changing. $dv = 0.079\text{V}$. This suggests the capacitor is still charging up toward the Zener limit.
    *   If $C_1$ is too large, it takes too long to reach the settled state ($dv \le 0.02\text{V}$).
    *   If $C_1$ is too small, the ripple $v_{pp}$ is too high.
    *   This is a classic trade-off. To fix $v_{pp}$, we need more $C_1$. To fix $dv$, we need a faster settling time (which means smaller $C_1$ or higher charging current).
    *   But wait, the charging current is limited by the piezo and the Zener.
    *   Wait, if the voltage is clamped by the Zener at $3.3\text{V}$, then $v_{avg}$ will eventually settle at the Zener voltage minus some drop.
    *   Is there a way to get more current into the capacitor to speed up settling?
    *   Or, can we lower the settled voltage so it's not fighting the Zener?
    *   The Zener is there to prevent $v_{max} > 3.6\text{V}$. S3 (strong excitation, light load) would definitely exceed $3.6\text{V}$ without the Zener.
    *   In S3, $v_{avg}$ is $3.4\text{V}$, $v_{max}$ is $3.41\text{V}$. The Zener is doing its job.
    *   In S2, $v_{avg}$ is $3.28\text{V}$, $v_{max}$ is $3.31\text{V}$.

    *   Maybe we can use a different way to limit the voltage? A Zener is a hard clamp.
    *   Alternatively, maybe the `SSHI_FullBridge` needs a different inductor/switch configuration?
    *   Let's try to move the inductor. Instead of the "flipping" circuit being a parallel branch, maybe a "buck-boost" like structure? No, the SYNC controller is designed for flipping (zero-crossings).
    *   Wait, the current `SSHI_FullBridge` is:
        - Full Bridge (D1, D2, D3, D4)
        - L1 from pzp to n1
        - S1 from n1 to pzn
    *   This flips the voltage across the piezo. This is the standard SSHI.
    *   If the only problem is the ripple and settling time in S2 (heavy load), let's consider if we can increase the effective energy extracted.
    *   The SSHI current is $I = V_{pzo} / (R_{on} + \dots)$.
    *   Maybe a different rectifier? The DSCH diodes have a drop.
    *   A synchronous rectifier would be better, but we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
    *   We already used 1 SYNC and 1 switch for the SSHI.
    *   We could use 2 SYNCs and 4 switches to make a synchronous rectifier, but then we lose the SSHI flipping.
    *   Is the SSHI flipping more valuable than the diode drop? Yes, usually.
    *   Wait, the `SSHI_FullBridge` used 1 switch. We can use more switches!
    *   What if we use 2 switches for the SSHI?
    *   In the current `SSHI_FullBridge`, the flipping is only done when $S_1$ is closed. The inductor $L_1$ is in series with the switch.
    *   $S_1$ closes at both edges. When $V_{pzo}$ is max, $L_1$ charges, then $S_1$ opens.
    *   Actually, the provided `SSHI_FullBridge` connectivity is: `L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn)`. This means the inductor and switch are in series across the piezo. This is the correct way to flip.

    *   Is there another topology?
    *   What if we use a "Voltage Doubler" (Dickson charge pump) style?
    *   Piezo $\to$ C-split $\to$ Rectifier.
    *   But SSHI is generally more efficient for piezos.
    *   Let's look at the `SSHI_FullBridge` failure again. $dv$ and $v_{pp}$ for S2.
    *   S2: $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$. $v_{avg} = 3.28\text{V}$.
    *   Power delivered to load: $P = V^2 / R_L = 3.28^2 / 150\text{k} = 71.7\mu\text{W}$.
    *   The measured $P_{load}$ is $71.6\mu\text{W}$. Correct.
    *   The $v_{pp}$ is $74\text{mV}$.
    *   $v_{pp} \approx \Delta V = I_{load} \cdot T / C_{out} = (3.28\text{V} / 150\text{k}\Omega) \cdot (1/100\text{Hz}) / 1.8\mu\text{F} = 21.8\mu\text{A} \cdot 0.01\text{s} / 1.8\mu\text{F} = 121\text{mV}$.
    *   Wait, the actual $v_{pp}$ is $74\text{mV}$, which is better than $121\text{mV}$. This is because the rectifier is charging the capacitor during the cycle.
    *   To get $v_{pp} < 50\text{mV}$, we need $C_{out}$ to be larger.
    *   $C_{out} \approx (I_{load} \cdot T) / \Delta V = (21.8\mu\text{A} \cdot 0.01\text{s}) / 0.05\text{V} = 4.36\mu\text{F}$.
    *   If we increase $C_{out}$ to $4.36\mu\text{F}$, will $dv$ (settled) be okay?
    *   $dv$ is the difference in mean voltage between 0.6-0.7s and 0.7-0.8s.
    *   If the voltage is still rising toward the Zener limit, $dv$ will be positive.
    *   The time constant to reach the Zener limit is $\tau = C_{out} / G_{charging}$.
    *   If we increase $C_{out}$, $\tau$ increases, and $dv$ will increase (fail).
    *   This is the core problem: $C_{out}$ must be large enough for ripple, but small enough for settling.
    *   Wait! If the Zener is clamping at $3.3\text{V}$, then $v_{avg}$ will be very close to $3.3\text{V}$.
    *   If we can't change $C_{out}$, can we change the Zener?
    *   The DZ33 zener breaks down at $3.3\text{V}$. If we replace it with a higher zener? No, $v_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$. A $3.3\text{V}$ zener is actually perfect.
    *   Is there another way to limit the voltage without a zener? A linear regulator (LDO)? Not available.
    *   What if we use a different SSHI technique that provides more power, so the voltage reaches the equilibrium faster?
    *   Or, what if we use a different $L$-$C$ flipping circuit?
    *   Let's try a "S-SSHI" (Series-SSHI). In S-SSHI, the flipping inductor is in series with the rectifier.
    *   Wait, let's try to improve the current `SSHI_FullBridge` by adding a second inductor/switch to flip the other side? No, we only have 2 SYNCs.
    *   What if we use a "Half-Bridge" SSHI but with a better rectifier?
    *   Looking at the results, the `SSHI_FullBridge` is very strong. Let's try to refine it.
    *   Is there any other way to reduce $v_{pp}$ without increasing $C_{out}$?
    *   Maybe a second capacitor in a different configuration?
    *   What if we use a "Capacitor-based" SSHI (SC-SSHI)? That uses switches and capacitors instead of an inductor.
    *   Wait, I have an idea. The $dv$ failure is because the voltage is still climbing toward the Zener limit.
    *   What if we lower the target voltage? If the voltage settles at $2.5\text{V}$ instead of $3.3\text{V}$, then $v_{pp}$ will be smaller (because $I_{load}$ is smaller) and $dv$ will be smaller (because it's not fighting the Zener).
    *   But the SSHI and the bridge rectifier will always push the voltage as high as the piezo open-circuit voltage (which is $\sim 3.2\text{V}$ amplitude, so $\sim 6.4\text{V}$ peak-to-peak). The Zener is the only thing keeping it down.
    *   If we can't change the Zener and we can't change $C_{out}$ too much, we need to increase the charging current to settle faster.
    *   But the charging current is limited by the piezo.
